financial-accounting.overview: Financial Accounting & Reporting under IFRS (Weygandt/Kimmel). Built from your resume (Ch 1–11), the Ch 14 cash-flow summary and the Ch 15 slides. Exam formula sheet: FHNW_FAR Formulae.pdf (provided in the exam).

summary.heading: Ch 1 · Accounting in action
points: Accounting has three activities: 1) identify the economic events of the business, 2) record them, 3) communicate them by preparing accounting reports.
Laws only set very generic standards, so companies follow a framework: GAAP (US standard) or IFRS (international standard, used in Europe and beyond).
Historical cost principle: record assets at their cost. Fair value principle: some assets are reported at their fair (market) value.
Relevance: financial information is capable of making a difference in a decision. Faithful representation: the information shows what really happened (complete, neutral, free from error).
Monetary unit assumption: only transaction data that can be expressed in money is recorded (e.g. the value of employees can't be measured).
Economic entity assumption: the business's activities are kept separate from those of its owners and other entities.
Equity grows with revenues and falls with expenses and dividends.

terms.def: resources a business owns: what do you own?
claims against assets: existing debts and obligations
the ownership claims on a company's total assets
cash, short-term investments, accounts receivable, inventory, prepaid expenses, equipment, buildings, intangible assets (e.g. licences)
accounts payable (invoices), short-term loans, taxes payable, mortgages payable, long-term loans
share capital + retained earnings

summary.heading: Ch 2 · The recording process
points: An account is the individual record of increases and decreases in a specific asset, liability or equity item.
Three parts of an account (T-account): 1) title, 2) left or debit side, 3) right or credit side.
Journalizing: 1) analyse the transaction, 2) enter it in the journal, 3) transfer (post) the journal information to the ledger accounts.
Debits and credits are summed up at the end of the day — easier than the Swiss system. One Cash account is used for all transactions (no split between bank, post and cash).
The ledger is the entire group of accounts a company keeps — like an account statement. Show the balance on the side that has more.
Trial balance: list of all accounts with their balances at a given time. It should balance (total debits = total credits).
Supplies: items bought to be consumed by the company (e.g. toilet paper).
Unearned service revenue: a service that has not been provided yet, but the money has already been received (a liability).

terms.def: assets, expenses, dividends
liabilities, share capital, retained earnings, revenues

summary.heading: Ch 3 · Adjusting the accounts
points: Time period assumption: accountants divide the economic life of a business into artificial periods (month, quarter, year). Monthly and quarterly periods are interim periods; large companies prepare both quarterly and annual statements. A fiscal year is one year long (sometimes 52–53 weeks).
Accrual-basis accounting (IFRS): transactions are recorded in the periods in which the events occur — revenue when the service is performed, expenses when incurred.
Cash-basis accounting (not IFRS): revenue when cash is received, expenses when cash is paid.
Adjusting entries make sure the revenue and expense recognition principles are followed. They are required every time financial statements are prepared.
Every adjusting entry includes one income statement account and one statement of financial position account.

Deferrals (cash first, service after): prepaid expenses (paid in advance, service received later: rent, insurance, supplies) and unearned revenues (cash received first, service promised for the future).
Accruals (service first, cash after): accrued revenues (service performed, revenue received later) and accrued expenses (service consumed first, paid later).

Depreciation (equipment, cars, infrastructure) is an allocation concept, not a valuation concept: it spreads an asset's cost over the periods it is used and does not report the actual change in value.

Statement presentation: a contra account (Accumulated Depreciation) shows both the cost of the equipment and the total cost expensed to date. Book (carrying) value = cost − accumulated depreciation, e.g. ₺5,000 − ₺40 = ₺4,960.
Unearned revenues: before adjustment, liabilities are overstated and revenues understated.
Accrued revenues: before adjustment, both assets and revenues are understated → adjustment increases an asset and a revenue.
Accrued expenses: before adjustment, both liabilities and expenses are understated → adjustment debits an expense and credits a liability.

Reminders: adjusting entries never involve Cash; check the adjustment makes sense (supplies used should increase Supplies Expense); double-check all computations; each entry affects one balance sheet and one income statement account.
Adjusted trial balance: shows all balances including adjustments, proves debits = credits after adjustments, and is the main basis for the financial statements (Cash, for example, doesn't change).
There are no strict rules on how to present the financial statements. Retained earnings change only with net profit and dividends.

examples.q: Yazici bought supplies for ₺2,500 on 5 Oct; ₺1,000 are still on hand on 31 Oct. Adjustment?
examples.a: Supplies used = 2,500 − 1,000 = ₺1,500 → Dr Supplies Expense 1,500 / Cr Supplies 1,500.

examples.q: ₺600 paid on 4 Oct for a one-year fire insurance policy starting 1 Oct. Adjustment for October?
examples.a: 600 / 12 = ₺50 → Dr Insurance Expense 50 / Cr Prepaid Insurance 50.

examples.q: Equipment depreciation is ₺480 a year. Adjustment for October?
examples.a: 480 / 12 = ₺40 → Dr Depreciation Expense 40 / Cr Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment 40.

examples.q: ₺1,200 received on 2 Oct for advertising to be completed by 31 Dec. How do you adjust?
examples.a: Record the part of the service performed in October: Dr Unearned Service Revenue / Cr Service Revenue (₺400 in the textbook example).

examples.q: Services worth ₺200 performed in October but not billed. Adjustment?
examples.a: Dr Accounts Receivable 200 / Cr Service Revenue 200.

examples.q: 3-month note payable of ₺5,000 at 12% signed 1 Oct. Interest for October?
examples.a: 5,000 × 12% × 1/12 = ₺50 → Dr Interest Expense 50 / Cr Interest Payable 50.

examples.q: Wages ₺2,000 for a 5-day week (₺400/day), last paid 26 Oct; 3 days unpaid on 31 Oct. Adjustment?
examples.a: 400 × 3 = ₺1,200 → Dr Salaries and Wages Expense 1,200 / Cr Salaries and Wages Payable 1,200.

summary.heading: Ch 4 · Completing the accounting cycle
points: Temporary accounts (revenues, expenses, dividends) are set to a balance of 0 at the end of the period — always closed. Permanent accounts (statement of financial position) are never closed.
Closing entries transfer net income or net loss and dividends to retained earnings.
Post-closing trial balance: contains only permanent accounts.
Miscellaneous expense: an account for general expenses.

Correcting entries are an avoidable step: unnecessary if records are free of errors, made whenever an error is discovered, and posted before closing entries. Alternative: reverse the incorrect entry and then record the correct one (neutralise the mistake).
Classified statement of financial position: a snapshot at a point in time; similar assets and liabilities are grouped to help users understand it.
Goodwill: the established reputation of a business, regarded as a quantifiable asset and calculated as part of its value when it is sold.

terms.def: capitalised development costs, goodwill, other intangibles
land, buildings, structures, machinery, vehicles, other — less accumulated depreciation
stocks and bonds of other companies held for many years; non-marketable equity investments

expected to be converted to cash or used up within one year or the operating cycle: inventories, trade and other receivables, derivative financial instruments, current tax assets, short-term investments, cash and cash equivalents
share capital – ordinary; retained earnings
due after one year: long-term debt, pension commitments, provisions, deferred tax liabilities, other

due within the coming year (long-term obligations become current ones): trade payables, current provisions, other current financial liabilities, income taxes payable, current maturities of long-term debt, other

summary.heading: Ch 5 · Merchandising operations
points: Merchandising companies buy and sell goods; their main revenue is sales revenue (sales). Operating expenses: rent, people, etc.
Perpetual system: detailed records of each purchase and sale; records continuously show inventory on hand; COGS is determined each time a sale occurs (a lot of effort with many transactions).
Periodic system: no detailed records during the period; COGS is determined at the end by a count — during the period you don't know the exact amount.

Purchases (perpetual): made with cash or on credit, recorded when goods are received; a purchase invoice supports each credit purchase. Inventory is always the account used for purchases of merchandise.

Freight: FOB + address = up to which point the seller is responsible. FOB shipping point → the buyer pays freight. FOB destination → the seller pays; the seller's cost is an operating expense (Freight-out).
Purchase returns (goods sent back) and purchase allowances (price reduction) when goods are damaged or defective.
Purchase discounts: credit terms may give a cash discount for prompt payment — the buyer saves money and the seller converts receivables to cash sooner. Account used: Inventory.
Sales may be on credit or for cash; revenue is recorded when the performance obligation is satisfied (goods transferred to the buyer). A sales invoice supports each credit sale.

Sales returns and allowances: the 'flip side' of purchase returns; a contra-revenue account (debit). Sales isn't debited directly, as that would hide the importance of returns as a % of sales and distort comparisons.
Sales discounts: offered to promote prompt payment; also a contra-revenue account.
Adjusting entries are needed for goods that were stolen or forgotten (inventory shrinkage).
Operating expenses: everything needed to run the business — salaries, utilities, advertising…

Other income and expense: items unrelated to the main line of operations (not the core business). Other income: interest revenue, dividend revenue, rent revenue, gain on sale of PP&E. Other expense: casualty losses (vandalism, accidents), loss on sale or abandonment of PP&E, losses from strikes. Interest expense, if material, must be shown on the face of the income statement.
Number of transactions = number of documents.
formulas: Beginning inventory + Cost of goods purchased = Cost of goods available for sale
Cost of goods available for sale − Ending inventory = Cost of goods sold
Gross profit rate = Gross profit / Net sales

summary.heading: Ch 6 · Inventories
points: Why count inventory physically? Perpetual system: 1) check the accuracy of the records, 2) find inventory lost to waste, shoplifting or employee theft. Periodic system: 1) determine inventory on hand, 2) determine COGS for the period.
Counting, weighing or measuring each kind of inventory — when the business is closed or slow, at the end of the period.
Goods in transit (purchased but not received, sold but not delivered) belong to the company with legal title, set by the terms of sale.
Consigned goods: you hold and try to sell someone else's goods for a fee without owning them (e.g. a co-op showing products) — they are not your inventory.
Specific identification: each item in inventory is costed individually — relatively rare (musical instruments, art). Most companies use cost flow assumptions.

FIFO: the costs of the earliest goods purchased are the first recognised in COGS; often parallels the physical flow. Ending inventory = unit cost of the most recent purchase, working backward until all units are costed.

Average-cost: allocates cost of goods available for sale using the weighted-average unit cost, applied to units on hand; assumes goods are similar. The cost flow doesn't need to match the physical movement of goods.
LCNRV: always take the lower of cost and net realisable value.
Inventory management is a double-edged sword: high levels → high carrying costs; low levels → stock-outs and lost sales.

summary.heading: Ch 8 · Receivables
points: Receivables are amounts due from individuals and companies, expected to be collected in cash — one of a company's most liquid assets. Managing them is very important for any company selling on credit.
Three types: accounts receivable, notes receivable, other receivables.
Recognising: a service company when it performs the service on account; a merchandiser at the point of sale on account. Sellers may offer discounts for early payment; returns reduce receivables.
Valuation: reported as a current asset at net (cash) realisable value = the net amount expected to be received in cash.
Sales on account create the risk of non-collection; losses are recorded as Bad Debt Expense (uncollectible accounts expense).

Direct write-off method: Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Accounts Receivable when an account is actually uncollectible. No matching of expenses with revenues, receivables not at cash realisable value → not acceptable for financial reporting (not accepted internationally).

Allowance method (required): estimate uncollectible accounts at the end of each period → Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts (a reserve for receivables). Better matching; receivables at cash realisable value.
Write-off under the allowance method: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts / Cr Accounts Receivable. It affects only balance sheet accounts and the cash realisable value stays the same.
Segregation of duties: the employee who writes off accounts should have no daily duties related to cash or receivables.
Recovery of an uncollectible account: reverse the write-off, then record the cash collection.
Percentage-of-receivables basis: management sets a % relationship between receivables and expected losses. Bad debt expense = required balance − existing balance in the allowance account.
Why sell receivables? 1) they may be the only reasonable source of cash, 2) billing and collection are time-consuming and costly.
Factor: a finance company or bank that buys receivables and collects directly from customers; fee usually 1–3%.

National credit card sales: the retailer pays the issuer 2–4% and records them as cash sales. Advantages: the issuer checks credit, keeps customer accounts, collects and absorbs losses; the retailer gets cash faster.

Promissory note: a written promise to pay a specified amount on demand or at a definite time — used when lending/borrowing, when amount and credit period exceed normal limits, or to settle accounts receivable. Maturity date: on demand, on a stated date, or at the end of a stated period; terms in months or days.
Short-term notes receivable are reported at cash realisable value; estimates are similar to accounts receivable.
formulas: Cash realisable value = Accounts receivable − Allowance for doubtful accounts
Average collection period = 365 / Accounts receivable turnover

summary.heading: Ch 9 · Plant assets and intangibles
points: Plant assets have physical substance, are used in operations, are not for sale to customers, and are useful for several years (unlike land, they decline in service potential). They play a key role.
Historical cost principle: record plant assets at cost = all expenditures necessary to acquire the asset and make it ready for its intended use (value at the time of purchase).
Land: all costs to make land ready increase (debit) Land — cash price, closing costs (title, attorney's fees), broker's commissions, accrued property taxes and liens assumed.
Land improvements: structural additions with limited lives (driveways, parking lots, fences, landscaping, sprinklers) — expensed over their useful lives.

Buildings: all costs related to purchase (price, closing costs, broker's commission, remodelling roof, floors, wiring, plumbing) or construction (contract price, architects' fees, permits, excavation).
Equipment: cash price, sales taxes, freight, insurance during transit paid by the buyer, assembling, installing and testing. Insurance and licences during use are not included — they recur.
Ordinary repairs maintain efficiency and productive life → Dr Maintenance and Repairs Expense (revenue expenditures).
Additions and improvements increase efficiency, capacity or useful life → Dr the plant asset (capital expenditures).

Depreciation: allocating the cost of a plant asset to expense over its useful life in a rational, systematic way — cost allocation, not valuation. Applies to land improvements, buildings, equipment; NOT land (its usefulness stays intact). Three factors: cost, useful life, residual value (estimate at end of life).

Straight-line: same amount each year; doesn't consider actual use. Units-of-activity (units-of-production): expense varies with use, e.g. cars, machine hours. Declining-balance: accelerated method, decreasing expense; double-declining rate = 2 × straight-line rate, applied to book value.

Disposals: 1) Retirement — scrapped, no cash, asset fully depreciated: Dr Accumulated Depreciation, Cr asset at cost. 2) Sale — compare price with book value: higher → gain, lower → loss. 3) Exchange — traded for new equipment. Always record depreciation up to the disposal date, then remove the asset (Dr Accumulated Depreciation, Cr asset).

Intangible assets: rights, privileges and competitive advantages from long-lived assets without physical substance — patents, copyrights, franchises and licences, trademarks, trade names, goodwill. Recorded at cost. Limited life → amortise (Cr the asset or Accumulated Amortisation). Indefinite life → no amortisation.
formulas: Units-of-activity = Depreciable cost / Total units × Units used

summary.heading: Ch 10–11 · Current and non-current liabilities
points: Current liability: a debt expected to be paid within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer.
Notes payable: written promissory note, usually with interest, often for short-term financing; current if due within one year of the statement date.
Other current liabilities: accounts payable, unearned revenues, accrued liabilities (taxes, salaries and wages, interest payable).

Value-added tax (VAT): most countries have a consumption tax to raise government revenue, paid by the final consumer. VAT is collected every time a business buys from another business in the supply chain; sales tax is collected only once, at the consumer's point of purchase.
Sales taxes payable: a stated % of the sales price; the seller collects it from the customer and pays it to the tax authority.
Current maturities of long-term debt: the part due this year; no adjusting entry — at the statement date, all obligations due within one year are classified as current.

Provision: recognise an expense and liability only if 1) there is a present obligation from a past event, 2) an outflow of resources is probable (more likely than not), 3) the amount can be reliably estimated.
Product warranties: estimated future costs of repairing or replacing units are expensed in the period of the sale.
Liquidity: the ability to pay maturing obligations and meet unexpected cash needs. The current ratio compares liquidity across companies of different sizes and over time — above 1 is good.
formulas: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities

summary.heading: Ch 12 · Equity and shares
points: Self-study with the intro video and self-assignment (23 Nov). Your resume doesn't have notes for this chapter yet — they'll be added once you write them.

summary.heading: Ch 14 · Statement of cash flows
points: Operating activities ↔ current assets and current liabilities. Investing activities ↔ investments and non-current assets. Financing activities ↔ non-current liabilities and equity.
Indirect method: 1) net income, 2) add depreciation/amortisation, 3) add losses / deduct gains, 4) adjust for changes in non-cash current assets and current liabilities.
Increase in a current asset → subtract; decrease → add. Increase in a current liability → add; decrease → subtract.
Direct method: cash revenues − cash expenses (non-cash revenues and expenses are left out).

summary.heading: Ch 15 · Financial analysis
points: Horizontal (trend) analysis: evaluates a series of data over time to find the increase or decrease, as an amount or a %. Applied to the statement of financial position, income statement and retained earnings statement.
Vertical (common-size) analysis: each item as a % of a base amount (total assets, net sales). Lets you compare companies of different sizes.
Ratio analysis: liquidity ratios (short-term ability to pay: current ratio, acid-test, AR turnover, inventory turnover), profitability and solvency ratios.

Example (Quality Department Store): current ratio 2.96:1 → €2.96 of current assets for every €1 of current liabilities; AR turnover 10.2 → collected every ~36 days; inventory turnover 2.3 → ~159 days in inventory.
formulas: Change since base period = (Current year − Base year) / Base year
Acid-test = (Cash + Short-term investments + Receivables) / Current liabilities
AR turnover = Net credit sales / Average net AR

IFRS: international standard (used in Europe). GAAP: US standard.

cards.a: Assets, expenses and dividends.

Liability: cash received before the service is performed.
Accrual: revenue when performed, expenses when incurred (IFRS). Cash: when cash moves (not IFRS).

cards.a: Deferrals: prepaid expenses, unearned revenues. Accruals: accrued revenues, accrued expenses.

cards.a: 5,000 × 12% × 1/12 = €50. Dr Interest Expense 50 / Cr Interest Payable 50.

Cost − Accumulated depreciation.

cards.a: Only permanent (statement of financial position) accounts.
An intangible asset: the established reputation of a business, recognised when a business is acquired.
Perpetual: COGS recorded at each sale with detailed records. Periodic: COGS determined at period end by a count.
Beginning inventory + Purchases = Goods available for sale; − Ending inventory = COGS.

cards.a: The buyer (ownership passes when goods leave the seller).

cards.a: A contra-revenue account with a debit balance.
Gross profit / Net sales.
First-in, first-out: the earliest costs go to COGS first; ending inventory uses the most recent costs.

cards.a: Turnover = COGS / Average inventory. Days = 365 / Turnover.

cards.a: The consignor (owner), not the consignee who sells them.
Lower of cost and net realisable value: report inventory at the lower amount.

cards.a: It doesn't match bad debt expense with revenue and doesn't show receivables at cash realisable value.

cards.a: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts / Cr Accounts Receivable. Cash realisable value stays the same.
A finance company or bank that buys receivables and collects them, charging 1–3%.

cards.a: Land: its usefulness and revenue-producing ability stay intact.
Repairs: revenue expenditure (expense). Additions/improvements: capital expenditure (debit the asset).
(Cost − Residual value) / Useful life

VAT is collected at every stage of the supply chain; sales tax only once at the final sale.

cards.a: Operating, investing, financing activities.

cards.a: Net income + depreciation/amortisation + losses − gains ± changes in non-cash current assets and current liabilities.

cards.a: Subtract the increase.

questions.explain: Historical cost: assets are recorded at what they cost.

options: Dr Salaries Expense 1,200 / Cr Salaries Payable 1,200

Under FOB destination, freight costs are paid by…

organisational-behaviour.overview: Organisational Behaviour with Prof. Dr. Anita Graf (Mon 13:15–15:00, Olten). Built from your resume. Exam: Moopad, K-Prim and A+/− questions, 75 minutes, 60 points, no aids. Admission: 8 of 10 Moodle assignments submitted on time.

summary.heading: Learning as a key competence
points: Learning is a key competence for studies and the world of work: developing the ability to act — how to apply knowledge and how to behave — and keep developing your whole life (lifelong learning).
Behavioural anchors: motivated to learn new things and applies what has been learnt; recognises the need for and benefits of learning; can initiate, continue and organise learning.
Learning in an organisational context: personnel development, knowledge management, organisational learning.
You can shape how you learn.

summary.heading: Basics of learning
points: Two things are needed to move information into long-term memory: ATTENTION and ACTIVE PROCESSING.
Inside the brain, nerve cells are active and constantly create new neural connections. The stronger the connections, the faster, easier and more automatically they transmit signals.

Learning physically changes the brain: the brain is plastic, and everything we do 'rewires' it. Learning means remodelling networks — new knowledge is linked to previous knowledge. It takes time, dedication and repetition.
Learning-type myth: learning preference ≠ learning effectiveness; learning ≠ perceiving; learning ≠ memorising. What matters is using all the senses to learn actively.

Motivational-volitional factors (trusting in your learning): motivation to learn and achieve; attribution style ('success is due to how hard I try'); self-concepts relevant to learning (perception of your own abilities); self-control and self-regulation (pursuing a goal despite obstacles, deferring rewards).

summary.heading: Learning strategies and techniques
points: Learning strategies are action plans that help your learning: cognitive, metacognitive, motivational and resource-oriented. They build on the multi-store memory model: sensory memory → working memory → long-term memory.
Primary (cognitive) strategies engage with the content. Repetition/memorising keeps information in memory but is a surface strategy — no deep understanding.
Depth-oriented strategies make learning meaningful: organisational strategies (how you structure the material, e.g. mind maps) and elaboration (connect new information with what you already know).
Metacognitive strategies (middle layer): planning (what do I need to learn, which strategy?), monitoring (do I understand? test yourself), regulating (not working? adjust).
Secondary (resource) strategies create the right conditions to learn — focus, motivation, energy.
Wild (2005) distinguishes: memorisation/repetition (surface), organisation/structuring (depth), elaboration (depth).

Mind mapping: central topic with up to ~7 branches ('basic organising ideas'), keywords, colours and images. Good for notes, organising lectures and exam prep — works through visualisation and reducing material to essentials.
Concept maps: network-based, several central concepts with labelled links ('is an example of'). Take longer but force deeper processing.
PQ4R reading method: Preview, Questions, Read, Reflect, Recite, Review. Faster alternatives: key-word scanning, line shortening, slalom technique, finger-pacing.
Note-taking: linear (outlining) or non-linear (Cornell notes: keyword column + notes column + summary). Handwriting engages more brain networks and improves recall compared with typing.
Loci technique: link information to a sequence of familiar places (e.g. your route home) — good for lists, sequences and numbers.
Spaced repetition: review at increasing intervals (Ebbinghaus forgetting curve) instead of cramming, e.g. with a Leitner box flashcard system.
Practice testing: self-testing (flashcards, practice questions, your own exam questions) strengthens retrieval and retention more than passive review — very powerful.

summary.heading: Self-management
points: Resource-based learning strategies are practical expressions of self-management skills: the 'tools' students use to consciously employ internal and external resources.

Self-management competence: the willingness and capacity to take ownership of your life, shaping it to sustain performance capability, willingness to perform, well-being and balance over the long term. (Willingness = being prepared, eager or happy to do something.)
Dynamic core model — 1 Self-responsibility: be the architect of your own life; stand up for your needs, values, goals and boundaries.
2 Self-awareness: gain insight into yourself; realistically assess strengths and areas for development; know your values and attitudes.
3 Self-development: implement development steps; lifelong learning; try new things and expand your boundaries.
4 Goals: set effective personal and professional goals, concrete action plans, and harmony between them.
5 Time & information: focus on the essentials; minimise time-wasters, distractions and interruptions; use effective methods.
6 Physical & mental health: health-promoting behaviour; reduce stressors, use resources; realistic expectations.
7 Social relationships: relationships that nurture, support and inspire; use and contribute to social support; build networks.
8 Self-control & self-regulation: self-motivation and self-calming techniques; emotion management (joy, gratitude; less anger and frustration); see setbacks as learning opportunities.
9 Other aspects: personality traits that influence self-management (e.g. self-efficacy, resilience).

summary.heading: Time management
points: Three E's: Effectiveness — doing the right thing, working on the essentials (which result should be there at the end?). Efficiency — doing things correctly, with the correct methods. Energy — using your daily energy economically: know when you perform best.

Micro-breaks: deliberate short interruptions of 30 seconds to 5–10 minutes. Effects: concentration (refocus, stay alert longer), performance (prevent mental fatigue), health (relieve eyes, muscles, back and neck), stress (interrupt the stress cycle), motivation (new energy and freshness).
Methods to know: ALPEN, Eisenhower matrix, MoSCoW, Rule of Three, time blocking, deep work, 2-minute rule, eat the frog, Pomodoro.

ALPEN (planning and prioritising): A = Activities (write down tasks, deadlines, activities); L = Length (estimate time per task); P = Padding (buffer time — plan max 60% of your working day); E = Establish priorities (decide, limit scope, shorten, delegate); N = Note-taking/checking (at day's end compare planned vs done, move unfinished tasks).

Eisenhower principle: important + urgent → do immediately; important + not urgent → schedule and plan; not important + urgent → delegate if possible, otherwise do it quickly; not important + not urgent → delete.
Pomodoro: fixed work interval, then a short break; after 3–4 intervals take a longer break.

summary.heading: Stress management
points: Stress = tension or pressure that requires an adaptive response from the body.
Distress (negative): perceived as a burden or excessive demand; can cause anxiety and helplessness. Eustress (positive): perceived as a manageable challenge; can trigger motivation and productivity.
Important: handle distress and eustress consciously — balance activation and regeneration.

Stress triad — 1 Stressors: all demanding conditions in the environment that trigger a stress response (physical environment, body, performance and social stressors, life-changing events, critical transitions, chronic tension). Not every demand is a stressor.
2 Personal stress amplifiers: 'I put myself under stress by…' — motives, judgements, beliefs, inner drivers such as be strong, be perfect, be popular. The person feels they can't take a break.

3 Stress response on three levels: physical (faster heart rate and breathing), observable behaviour (skipping breaks, restlessness, eating/smoking more), cognitive-emotional (restlessness, helplessness, anxiety, carousel of thoughts).
De-skilling (AI): problem-solving capabilities erode when decisions are delegated entirely to algorithms.

summary.heading: Groups and teams
points: Collaboration: the ability to work effectively and synergistically in a team toward a common goal — coordinate, make sense of diversity, manage conflict, be open-minded.
Formal group: defined by the organisation's structure, roles or tasks (e.g. project teams). Informal group: voluntary — people choose to share or socialise.

Working group: members mainly exchange information so everyone has the knowledge (e.g. students finishing a project). Working team: coordinated collaboration to achieve a goal (e.g. implementing an IT system with people from other departments).
Size and performance: small groups process input effectively; 4–6 people is optimal; more than 6 brings more ideas and perspectives.
Risk: social loafing / free-riding when your own contribution isn't visible, the group is large or others' commitment is unclear → prevent it by defining exactly what everyone should do.
Roles: define each person's tasks; role expectations, role perception, multiple roles at once.
Belbin team roles (interaction of three): Plant (inventive, creative ideas), Coordinator (decision-making), Shaper/doer (implements the ideas). Diversity matters.

Five key requirements for effective teamwork: 1) clear communication, 2) definition of roles, 3) mutual respect, 4) effective problem-solving, 5) clear focus on objectives. Celebrating success is very important.

summary.heading: Conflict
points: Conflict: the experience of incompatibility between the beliefs or interests of at least two parties, and their activities to overcome this incompatibility by whatever means.
Disruption: temporary and easily resolved (someone forgot something, then work continues). Conflict: long-term and personal, needs more intensive solutions.

Causes: relationship conflicts (a person feels belittled or rejected — can damage self-esteem); evaluation conflicts (parties value a goal's importance differently); assessment conflicts (same goal, disagree on how to reach it); distribution conflicts (dispute over a scarce or indivisible resource).

Forms: latent (differences not yet hostile) vs open (the conflict has 'broken out'); hot (fierce arguing) vs cold (no outward dispute, anger and frustration repressed — mood cold, empty or cynical); strong (clear mutually exclusive pros and cons) vs weak (less pronounced positions).
Consequences: relationship and task conflicts both correlate negatively with member satisfaction (relationship conflicts strongly) and with group performance.
Conflict management: if the manager is part of the conflict, the more advanced the escalation, the more likely an independent expert is needed. If the manager is not part of it, they act as mediator.

Conflict regulation through: power (enforce a solution), rights — 'who is right?' (decide like a court), interests (both sides express interests → negotiation), self-regulation (the parties find the solution).
Strategies for positive cooperation: communication, cooperation, respect, trust, solution orientation, motivation and support.

summary.heading: Personality
points: Personality: the sum of an individual's ways of reacting and interacting. Personality psychology asks how and why people differ or are similar.
Described by measurable personality traits — relatively stable characteristics over time.
Determinants: disposition (factors fixed at conception) or environment? Typical research design: studies of identical twins.

Personality tests are used for personnel selection, job fit and career planning. Self-assessments (questionnaires) are common in applications; weaknesses: impression management and the situation. Research shows observer judgements predict job success better.
Personality models: the Big Five (OCEAN) — why they matter so much for predicting behaviour at work.
The dark triad (narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy): negative traits that often overlap and are partly correlated with professional success.
Exam tip from class: case III question uses K-Prim (true/false) answers.

summary.heading: Reflection
points: Reflect: the ability to challenge yourself, others and systems to enable constructive further development — identify underlying systems of behaviour, thought and values, assess their consequences and act accordingly. Needed almost everywhere in a company (e.g. adapting to new technologies) to keep improving decisions.

Success factors: make time and space; accept that reflection can be uncomfortable; use methods and guiding questions; integrate it into your routine; take other perspectives and feedback into account; document insights and turn them into action.
Four dimensions — level: individual (own behaviour, emotions, motives), team (collaboration, dynamics, communication), system (structures, processes, culture, governance).
Content: almost anything can be reflected on.
Depth: analytical (connections, causes and effects), evaluative (assess actions, draw conclusions and measures), transformative (critically re-examine your own beliefs and values).
Methods: start-stop-continue, 5W method, diary/journaling, Gibbs reflective cycle.

Gibbs cycle: Description (what happened, who was involved, how did it turn out?) → Feelings (how did you feel, what did you think?) → Evaluation (what went well or badly?) → Analysis (why did it turn out this way, causes?) → Conclusion (what did you learn, what would you do differently?) → Action plan (what will you do next time?).
Start-stop-continue: what should we start doing, stop doing, and continue doing?

summary.heading: Emotions
points: Affect: umbrella term. Emotion: relatively short and intense (seconds or minutes). Mood: much longer (hours or days), cause can't be identified. Feeling: can be described specifically.

Components of an emotion: cognitive (appraisal — the brain evaluates the situation immediately), physiological (bodily response, heart beats faster), motivational (readiness to act), expressive (face, tone of voice), subjective (feeling/experience).
Classification: circumplex model of emotions.
At work emotions are fundamental — they influence job performance, creativity, engagement, decision-making, collaboration and leadership, coping with challenges, health and well-being.

Affective events theory (Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996): work environment/job characteristics → affective work events → (with individual dispositions) affective reactions → work attitudes → judgement-driven behaviour (conscious evaluation) and affect-driven behaviour (spontaneous).
Emotion regulation: all processes that influence which emotions we have, when, and how we experience and express them. What can be influenced: type, onset, duration, experiential quality, expression.
Why regulate? Hedonic (want to feel good), instrumental (the situation requires it), prosocial (don't want to burden others).

Discrepancy perception is the central prerequisite: recognising that the current emotion doesn't match what you want or what the situation requires — needs emotion knowledge and knowledge of social norms.

Strategies targeting emotion elicitation: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment (focus on something that feels better), cognitive reappraisal (change how you think about the situation).
Strategies targeting the response: regulate physiological arousal, the feeling/subjective experience, and expressive behaviour.
Emotional labour: emotion regulation at work — feelings are deliberately induced or suppressed to create an outward display intended to have a particular effect on others.

summary.heading: Motivation
points: Motivation: the processes that determine the intensity, direction and persistence with which an individual strives to achieve a goal. It varies between and within people (time, situation) and links to performance.
Intensity: effort and concentration. Direction: clear how to achieve something. Persistence: how long you keep going (why some give up and others don't).
Motives as stable preferences for types of goals (McClelland, 1987): need for achievement, power, affiliation.
Equity theory (Adams, 1965) and organisational justice: social comparison of your inputs and outcomes with relevant others; distributive and procedural justice.
Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham, 1990): specific, challenging goals enhance performance; feedback during goal pursuit is essential.

Instrumentality model (Vroom, 1964), an expectancy-value theory refined as VIE (valence-instrumentality-expectancy): explains the quantity of motivation. Motivation depends on the expectancy that an action leads to an outcome and the value of that outcome; the outcome's value lies in being useful (instrumental) for further consequences.

Self-determination theory: about the quality of motivation; mini-theories on intrinsic motivation (how it can be undermined), extrinsic motivation (its internalisation) and three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness).
Intrinsic: the activity is to some extent an end in itself — feeling competent and autonomous, joy and interest, seeking optimal challenges. Extrinsic: effort for a goal beyond the activity.

Can rewards harm? Experiments: people work on interesting tasks, the experimental group gets rewards/feedback/competition; intrinsic motivation is measured by voluntary time on the task during a 'break'. Undermined by money, prizes, awards, (avoiding) punishment, controlling feedback, deadlines, competition (even when winning) — because competence and autonomy feel threatened.

Internalisation of extrinsic motivation: not everything has to be fun — recognising its necessity is often enough. Support it by acknowledging the other's perspective, explaining why it matters, providing choices, giving informative non-controlling feedback.
Qualities of motivation: external regulation (someone tells you) → introjected (pressure, self-esteem) → identified (you accept the value) → intrinsic (you enjoy it).

Leaders can: encourage initiative and growth, welcome criticism, accept mistakes, give informative feedback, support individuality, require respect, show the bigger picture, refer to shared values, give meaningful choices.

summary.heading: Perception
points: Perception: how individuals organise and interpret sensory impressions so their environment makes sense. Behaviour is based on subjective perception, not reality itself — and perception can differ significantly from objective reality.
Process: environmental stimuli → sensory input → neural processing → perception (interpretation) → recognition (categorising).
Bottom-up processing: data/stimulus-driven. Top-down: knowledge-driven (knowledge, expectations, motivation, intentions).
Selective attention influences many stages. Selective perception is shaped by experience, expectations, motives and context → two people can experience the same situation differently.
Biases I — halo and horns: one characteristic overshadows the overall judgement (positive = halo, negative = horns). At work: attractive people often get better appraisals and are hired more.
Biases II — contrast effect: people we met just before influence our judgement. Average candidates are rated lower after strong ones and higher after weak ones.
Biases III — similar-to-me effect: rating people more positively when they seem similar. Similar supervisor–subordinate pairs: more liking and better evaluations; dissimilarity: more role ambiguity.
Biases IV — stereotypes: simplified, generalised beliefs about members of a social group; influence recruiting, appraisals and perceived leadership competence.

Self-image: your own view of your abilities and characteristics, shaped by experience, feedback and social comparison; affects confidence and ambition. External image: how others see us, shaped by visible characteristics, first impressions, stereotypes and context/role.

Johari window: shows conscious and unconscious, visible and hidden parts of personality; reveals gaps between self-image and external image; promotes feedback and self-reflection; goal = more trust, fewer blind spots.
Attribution theory: is behaviour explained by internal causes (personality) or external causes (the situation)?
Kelley's covariation model: consensus (do others behave the same?), distinctiveness (is it specific to this situation?), consistency (does it recur over time?).
Fundamental attribution error: judging others, we underestimate external factors and overestimate internal ones. Self-serving bias: our successes → internal factors, failures → external factors.

summary.heading: Decision-making
points: Decide: recognise the need for a decision, consider perspectives, weigh options, make the decision and defend it.
Dilemma: several goals, values or interests conflict and no option can satisfy them all.
Decision-making: choosing between at least two options to achieve desired outcomes and avoid undesired ones; the choice forms the intention to implement it.
1 Rational model ('homo economicus'): considers all information, identifies all options without bias, chooses the greatest benefit — never 100% possible.
2 Bounded rationality: limited time, information and cognitive capacity; problems are simplified, people settle for a good-enough solution → satisficing.
3 Intuition: unconscious, based on experience, patterns and emotions; quick in uncertain or complex situations; should be supplemented by facts and analysis.

Group decision-making — benefits: diversity of ideas and knowledge, better risk management, more acceptance and commitment, learning. Disadvantages: more time and resources, conflicts, groupthink and conformity.
Heuristics: mental shortcuts. Biases: errors of judgement.
Overconfidence: overestimating abilities or knowledge — strong in people with little experience, but managers and experts too; most think they're less biased than others.
Confirmation bias: seeking information that confirms existing views; personalised algorithms and AI can reinforce this (echo chambers).
Anchoring: relying on the first figure given, even if irrelevant — typical in wage and price negotiations and investments.
Availability bias: events seem more likely if examples come to mind easily — media shape risk perception.
Escalation of commitment: sticking with a failing decision because time, money or resources were already invested.
Risk and loss aversion: prefer certain gains; losses weigh more than equal gains; to avoid losses people take bigger risks. Framing effect: how a decision is presented changes risk appetite.
Hindsight bias: believing you foresaw an outcome. Outcome bias: judging a decision by its result instead of the process.
Better decisions despite biases: define objectives, question assumptions, evaluate more options.

AI: opportunities — fast data analysis and pattern recognition; human–AI collaboration improves and speeds decisions. Risks — over-trust, inherited and reinforced bias from training data, wrong information, confirming existing beliefs.

summary.heading: Concept of thinking
points: Thinking is innate — something we have inside us.

System 1 — fast thinking: intuitive, often unconscious, fast and efficient, based on knowledge, experience and established mental models; more susceptible to cognitive biases. We react without thinking (saying hello).

System 2 — slow thinking: analytic, deliberate conscious reasoning, slow; typical of critical thinking and structured analytic techniques; used with qualitative and quantitative methods (buying a house, choosing your studies or job).

summary.heading: What is critical thinking?
points: Critical does not mean negative.
Analyse information and arguments carefully with a critical eye, and look at things from different perspectives and angles. Some people find this uncomfortable.
Definition: critical thinking is the art of analysing and evaluating thinking with a view to improving it.
Obstacles: too much thinking; not enough time (or underestimating the time needed); stopping to think because of AI; information overload; emotions; lack of practice, skills or freedom.

summary.heading: Media & information literacy I: assessing sources
points: Assess sources and information by: authorship, format, audience, content, purpose.
Everyday vs academic sources: academic sources are peer-reviewed, written for a scholarly audience, have a full bibliography, and are considered credible.
Types of sources: print (newspapers, magazines, books), broadcast (TV, radio, films), digital/online media (websites, social media, apps).

Information disorder (Shu et al., 2020): misinformation = false content shared by someone who doesn't realise it's false (intent not always malicious: false information, urban legends). Disinformation = fake or inaccurate information intentionally spread to mislead or deceive (fake news, fabricated content). Malinformation = genuine information shared to cause harm (hate speech, harassment).

summary.heading: Media & information literacy II
points: Lateral reading: don't trust the first source — check what multiple other sources say.

Media literacy: 'a set of competencies that enable us to interpret media texts and institutions, to make media of our own, and to recognize and engage with the social and political influence of media in everyday life.'

Public service media: made, financed and controlled by the public, for the public; neither commercial nor state-owned; free from political interference and commercial pressure → independence. Still, be careful with the information transmitted.

Functions of the media: entertain and provide an outlet for imagination; educate and inform; serve as a public forum for important issues; act as a watchdog for government, business and other institutions.
Free speech: the right to express your opinions publicly. Free press: newspapers, magazines, TV and radio can express any opinion, even criticising the government and other organisations.

Social media: filter bubbles — intellectual isolation created by algorithms that personalise content from your past behaviour (clicks, likes, searches) without you choosing it; echo chambers — you are mainly exposed to opinions that reinforce your beliefs, the same content again and again; algorithms drive both.

Investigative journalism uncovers wrongdoing (corruption, misconduct) in government and business: it goes beyond official statements, reveals what happens behind the scenes, is the 'conscience' of journalism and a check on power — sometimes the last trusted institution where courts or oversight bodies fail. Useful tool: ground.news.
Facts vs opinions (important): academic writing must be verified by sources. A fact is objective, discovered, states reality and can be proved or verified.

summary.heading: Scientific quality criteria
points: Basic belief: we can never know with absolute certainty whether our findings correspond to reality.

Critical rationalism: critique as a principle — based on observation, checking for self-contradictions and contradictions with empirical-scientific theories, and monitoring success in solving the problem. Drives human creativity, imagination and curiosity.

Critically evaluating results: is the evidence authentic (origin)? are there similar findings elsewhere? were the conditions realistic and valid? could the research be distorted? are there biases in the survey or measurements?

summary.heading: Argumentation and fallacies
points: An argument has a claim and a reason. Example — claim: people should be allowed to smoke anywhere; reason: smoking isn't illegal and millions enjoy it.
Fallacies: false or unsound arguments where the next logical step isn't followed — ideas people think are true but aren't.

summary.heading: Research questions and the research paper
points: 1 Introduction: research context, research gap, research question, thesis (the authors' position), aim.
2 Literature review: what we know today — what other researchers have said so far.
3 Research approach (method).
4 Findings.
5 Discussion: combine your findings with previous findings.
6 Conclusion.

Inductive reasoning: specific observation → pattern recognition → general conclusion. Deductive reasoning: existing theory → hypothesis → collect data → analyse data → do or don't reject the hypothesis.

DOI (Digital Object Identifier): shown on the article to identify it permanently.

principles-of-management.overview: Principles of Management (Thu 17:30–21:00), textbook chapters 1–7, 10, 14 and 16. Built from your resume. The guest speaker on 10 Dec (Nathanael Hausmann, Läderach) is mandatory and exam-relevant.

summary.heading: Ch 1 · Management, functions and levels
points: Efficiency: using resources (people, money, raw materials) wisely to attain goals. Effectiveness: achieving results — making the right decisions and carrying them out successfully so the organisation reaches its goals.
Simple decisions or goals can be incredibly powerful (e.g. cosmetics, once only for women, now earn more by also targeting men).
Four principal functions (POLC): Planning, Organising, Leading, Controlling.

Levels (pyramid): top managers (the CEO looks 5–10 years ahead and translates that vision to the levels below — you must make people understand what you want), middle managers, first-line managers (department head, foreperson, supervisor).
Functional manager: responsible for one activity (finance director, HR administrator). General manager: several activities, usually supervises other managers.
Three types of organisations: for-profit, non-profit, mutual-benefit (aid their members) — managers are needed everywhere.

summary.heading: Ch 1 · Roles and skills of managers
points: Interpersonal roles: interact with people inside and outside the unit — figurehead, leader, liaison (between people, talking to media…).
Informational roles: receive and communicate information — monitor, disseminator, spokesperson.
Decisional roles: use information to solve problems or seize opportunities — entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator.
Conceptual skills: think analytically, see the organisation as a whole and how its parts work — understand why something happens and what is wrong, and improve the business.
Human skills: work well with others, especially in teams.
Technical skills: job-specific knowledge and techniques.

summary.heading: Ch 1 · Challenges and career readiness
points: Challenge 1 — competitive advantage (outperform others): innovation, efficiency, quality (e.g. Müller AG in South Africa: expensive but quality), responsiveness to customers.
Challenge 2 — information technology: e-commerce, rise of AI and automation, constant electronic management, organisational change in structure, jobs, goals and management.
Challenge 3 — diversity (gender, age, ethnicity…) can be a strength; the challenge is managing diverse employees to maximise their contributions.
Challenge 4 — globalisation: the increasingly interconnected world economy; culture matters, so understand and adapt to cultural differences.
Challenge 5 — ethical standards. Challenge 6 — the 17 Sustainable Development Goals. Challenge 7 — happiness and meaningfulness: people need to be happy and comfortable.
Career readiness: having the knowledge, skills and attributes employers want — knowledge (hard skills), soft skills, attitudes (learned predisposition toward objects, people or events).

Developing career readiness: 1) build self-awareness (feedback, validated self-assessments); 2) learn from courses; 3) model others (role models and mentors, observe, try new behaviours and discuss); 4) learn on the job (new assignments, represent management at meetings, coach others, lead a team or project); 5) student groups and organisations; 6) experiment (practise new behaviours, keep a journal).

summary.heading: Ch 2 · Classical viewpoint
points: Scientific management: applying the scientific study of work methods to improve worker productivity.

Frederick Taylor's four principles: 1) scientifically study each part of the task; 2) carefully select workers with the right abilities; 3) give workers training and incentives to use the proper methods; 4) use scientific principles to plan work methods and ease the way for workers.
Administrative management: managing the total organisation's productivity and efficiency.

Key lessons: think about the resources you really have and how to use them (McDonald's adding breakfast); don't follow every rule or theory — pick the best. There's no right or wrong: it depends on time, industry and people.

summary.heading: Ch 2 · Behavioural and quantitative viewpoints
points: Behavioural viewpoint: understand human behaviour and motivate employees toward achievement — early behaviourism, human relations movement, behavioural science.

Early behaviourism (more democratic): organisations as communities where managers and subordinates work in harmony; conflicts resolved by talking it through to satisfy both sides; work controlled by workers with the relevant knowledge, managers as facilitators.
Human relations movement: better human relations increase productivity.
Behavioural science: scientific research on human behaviour to give managers practical tools.

Quantitative management: statistics, computer simulations and other quantitative techniques for management. (Classical = work processes; behavioural = motivation and attitudes; quantitative = organisational processes.)

Operations management: managing production and delivery of products or services more effectively, especially the supply chain — from design and raw materials to the customer and even disposal or recycling.
Evidence-based management: translate principles based on the best evidence into practice, bringing rationality to decisions.

summary.heading: Ch 2 · Systems, contingency and contemporary approaches
points: Systems viewpoint: interrelated parts operating together for a common purpose. Closed system: little interaction with the environment. Open system: interacts with its environment (most organisations).
Synergy: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts (e.g. a band).
Complexity theory: how order and patterns arise from very complicated, apparently chaotic systems. Feedback from inside and outside is important (Google Glass failed).
Contingency viewpoint: the manager's approach should vary with the individual and the environmental situation.
Learning organisation: actively creates, acquires and transfers knowledge and changes behaviour to reflect it.
High-performance work practices (HPWPs): build employees' knowledge, skills and abilities (KSAs), improve motivation, and give opportunities to make important decisions and take responsibility.
Shared value and sustainable development: meet present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.

Career corner — 8 things to know before an interview: mission and vision; core values and culture; company history; key players; who interviews you; products, services and clients; current events and accomplishments; comments from current or former employees.

summary.heading: Ch 3 · Stakeholders and the environment
points: Shareholder value perspective: the company's purpose is to maximise value for shareholders (people who own shares/equity).
Stakeholder perspective: the corporation exists also for employees, suppliers, customers and society.
Triple bottom line: People, Planet, Profit.

Stakeholders' influence: resource provision (capital, skills, materials); decision influence (customers' preferences guide product development); accountability and oversight (owners monitor financial results); feedback and innovation.
Management's responsibility: identify relevant stakeholders; assess their influence and expectations; balance conflicting interests ethically and legally; communicate effectively to build trust.
PESTLE: trigger → challenge + evidence = consequence.

summary.heading: Ch 4 · Global management
points: Globalisation: the collapse of time and distance; you and international management; why and how companies expand internationally; free trade and regional economic cooperation; the value of understanding cultural differences. (Entry modes and global vs multidomestic strategy are in Ch 6.)

summary.heading: Ch 5 · Planning
points: Planning: setting goals and deciding how to achieve them — gives direction and reduces uncertainty (personal: weekly budget for a holiday; management: next quarter's sales targets and marketing).
Why plan? 1) direction and momentum, 2) encourage new ideas, 3) sustainable competitive advantage.
Strategic planning: top managers, long-term goals for the whole organisation. Tactical: middle managers, medium-term. Operational: first-line managers, short-term, day-to-day.
Means-end chain: how goals connect across the organisation.

Mission statement: purpose — why it exists and what it seeks to achieve. Vision statement: long-term aspiration (10–15 years) that motivates and can change (oil and gas moving toward sustainable sources). Values statement: core priorities, principles and beliefs guiding behaviour.
Goals/objectives: specific targets — strategic, tactical or operational.
SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Results-oriented, Target date.
Management by objectives (MBO): 1) set objectives together, 2) develop action plans, 3) review performance periodically, 4) evaluate and reward on results.
Planning/control cycle: continuously evaluate progress on strategic goals and adjust.
Single-use plans: for activities unlikely to repeat. Standing plans: for recurring activities.
Pitfalls: top-down planning (no employee involvement), overly rigid plans, failure to update. Improve with flexibility, involvement and continuous review.

summary.heading: Ch 6 · Strategic positioning and analysis
points: Strategic positioning: achieving sustainable competitive advantage by preserving what is distinctive about a company.

Porter's three principles: 1) a unique and valuable position (few needs/many customers, broad needs/few customers, broad needs/many customers) — different activities or the same ones done differently; 2) trade-offs — decide what not to do, you can't be everything to everyone; 3) fit among activities — they reinforce each other, making the strategy hard to copy.
Mission: why we exist. Vision: what we want to become.
Sustainable competitive advantage: competitors can't duplicate the value delivered.
Assessing current reality: competitive intelligence, SWOT, forecasting, benchmarking, VRIO.
SWOT: strengths, weaknesses (internal), opportunities, threats (external).
PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal): 1) assess the risks of entering new markets or starting a venture, 2) analyse the macro environment.

Forecasting: a projection of the future so managers can use and reallocate resources efficiently. Trend analysis: extending past events into the future. Scenario analysis: alternative, equally likely futures with a plan for each.
Benchmarking: comparing your performance with high-performing organisations.

summary.heading: Ch 6 · Corporate-level strategy
points: 1 Growth — concentration: invest all efforts in the existing business (improve products, develop and expand the brand, customer loyalty). Options: market penetration (more existing products in existing markets), market development (new regions or segments), product development (new or improved products for existing markets).

Vertical integration: take over activities along the supply chain. Backward = upstream (control suppliers); forward = downstream (control distribution/retail). Pros: control, lower costs, profitability, quality, secure supply, market insight. Cons: high investment, less flexibility, complex management, risk concentration, inefficiencies, cultural challenges.

Diversification: new products or markets to reduce dependence and spread risk. Related (linked, e.g. sportswear → fitness equipment, using brand/technology/customers) vs unrelated (a different industry, e.g. food → real estate, to spread financial risk).
International expansion — exporting: produce at home, sell abroad. + low investment and risk, tests demand. − tariffs, transport, currency; little control over marketing.
Licensing: a foreign firm uses your IP for royalties. + income with almost no capital, avoids trade barriers, local know-how. − little control over quality and brand; may create a future competitor.

Franchising: the full business model (brand, processes, training, support) for fees and royalties — McDonald's in Switzerland. + fast expansion, motivated local owners. − hard quality control, profits shared.

Joint venture: two companies create a jointly owned company, sharing equity, control, profits and risk. + local knowledge, networks, sometimes the only legal entry. − conflicts over control and profits; more investment and risk.

Wholly owned subsidiary (100%): greenfield (build new) or acquisition (buy existing). + full control, all profits, protects know-how. − highest investment and risk, slow, integration and cultural problems (Walmart with ASDA UK).

Global strategy (Coca-Cola): world as one market, standardised products, high integration, low local responsiveness, centralised decisions; + lower costs, strong brand, easy control; − less flexibility, poor cultural fit.

Multidomestic strategy (Nestlé adapts flavours, packaging, marketing): low integration, high local responsiveness, decentralised; + better customer fit, flexibility; − higher costs, weaker global brand, fewer economies of scale.
2 Stability: little or no change — when the environment is stable, the company performs well, market growth is low, or management consolidates before growing.

3 Defensive: reduce efforts to cut costs and restore profit — turnaround (LEGO 2004 cut products, back to the brick), divestiture (Novartis spun off Alcon 2019 and Sandoz 2023; Migros sold Hotelplan, SportX, Melectronics), liquidation (Toys "R" Us US, 2018), bankruptcy (court protection to restructure debts).
BCG matrix: portfolio tool — invest, develop or divest — based on market growth rate (industry attractiveness) and market share (competitive strength).

summary.heading: Ch 6 · Business-level strategy and implementation
points: Porter's five forces: 1) threat of new entrants, 2) bargaining power of suppliers (Netflix making its own content as licence fees rose), 3) bargaining power of buyers (informed customers negotiate better), 4) threat of substitutes, 5) rivalry among competitors. Recommendation: also do a SWOT.

Porter's four competitive strategies: cost leadership (lower costs/prices, wide market), differentiation (unique superior value, wide market), cost focus (low cost, narrow market), focused differentiation (unique value, narrow market).
Stuck in the middle: no clear strategy or trade-offs, weak cost control and innovation, no clear identity, weak brand and loyalty, below-average profits.

The choice depends on resources, capabilities, industry conditions and customer needs. Executive questions: what does the playing field look like? what has the competition been doing? what have you been doing? what's around the corner? what's your winning move?

Functional strategy: each department's plan to support higher-level strategies — corporate and business strategies decide what to do and how to compete; functional strategies decide how to do it best. Supporting value-chain activities: firm infrastructure, HR management, procurement.

Evaluating options with SAF: Suitability (fits goals, opportunities and threats?), Acceptability (meets stakeholders' expectations on risk and return?), Feasibility (realistic with available resources, skills and finances?).
Implementation: execution; three core processes — people (who will help you in the future), strategy (how success will be achieved), operations (which path to follow).
Roadblocks: misaligned culture, poor performance management and leadership, conflicting functional objectives, employees' resistance to change.
Strategic control: monitor implementation and act on results — engage people, keep it simple, stay focused, keep moving.

summary.heading: Ch 7 · Rational and nonrational decision making
points: Rational decision making — managers should make logical, optimal decisions in four stages: 1) identify the problem or opportunity, 2) think up alternative solutions (obvious and creative; brainstorm), 3) evaluate alternatives and select (is it ethical? feasible? ultimately effective — good enough now but not in the long run → reconsider), 4) implement and evaluate (plan carefully, be sensitive to those affected).
Law of unintended consequences: things happen that weren't foreseen → give it more time, change it slightly, try another alternative, or start over.

Nonrational decision making (how managers actually decide): bounded rationality (undermined by hindrances — obstacles), hubris (inflated pride), satisficing (seek alternatives until one is satisfactory, not optimal), intuition (choosing without conscious thought or logical inference).
Information overload: too much information for one person to process.

summary.heading: Ch 7 · Ethics, evidence and big data
points: Unethical behaviour matters more and more: people are less forgiving, regulations are stricter, expansion into developing countries brings higher ethical risk and weaker laws, digital communication increases exposure (whistleblowing), negative information spreads in real time.
Causes of ethical lapses: organisational level (poor board oversight), group level (intense commitment to the mission), individual level (a leader's personality and social characteristics).

Whistleblowing: reporting an employee's incorrect behaviour. Ethics officer: someone trained in ethical matters at work. Road map to ethical decisions: a decision tree (graph of decisions and their consequences).

Evidence-based decision making: gathering and analysing high-quality data to develop and implement a plan. Seven principles: treat your organisation as an unfinished prototype; no brag, just facts; see yourself as outsiders do; it's not only for senior executives; you still need to sell it; if all else fails, slow the spread of bad practice; best diagnostic question — what happens when people fail?
Big data: too large for a typical computer; 5 Vs — Volume, Variety, Velocity, Veracity, Value.

Descriptive analytics: trends in past data (Netflix suggests content from what you watched). Machine learning: algorithms detect patterns without explicit programming. Predictive analytics: historical data + statistical models to predict outcomes (weather forecast).
Big data helps meet customer needs, HR management (retention, training, rewards), production efficiency, and decisions at every level of the hierarchy (with training).

summary.heading: Ch 7 · AI, styles, biases and group decisions
points: AI types: automate (robotic AI, repetitive tasks), anticipate (algorithmic AI: match supply with demand, customise pricing, schedule maintenance), analyse (biometric AI, e.g. facial recognition), advise (conversational AI, chatbots). Benefit: enhance worker creativity. Drawbacks: implementation, data issues, cost.

Decision-making styles combine tolerance for ambiguity and value orientation (task/technical vs people/social): directive (low ambiguity tolerance, efficient, logical, practical), analytical (high tolerance, analyses a lot, slower), conceptual (high tolerance, people-oriented, long-term, many options), behavioural (most people-oriented, supportive, prefers verbal information).
Ten biases: availability, representativeness, confirmation, sunk cost, anchoring and adjustment, overconfidence, hindsight, framing, escalation of commitment, categorical thinking.
Groupthink: members agree too readily, become overconfident and stop thinking outside the box. Group decisions are less efficient, size affects quality, groups may be too confident, knowledge counts.

Consensus — do: listen, involve as many members as possible, find the reasons behind arguments, dig for facts. Don't: log-roll or horse-trade ('I'll support you if you support me'), agree just to keep the peace, vote (creates winners and losers).

Seven brainstorming rules: defer judgement; build on others' ideas ('and' not 'but'); encourage wild ideas; quantity over quality (best ideas come in the first two minutes); be visual; one conversation at a time; brainstorm questions, not answers.
Also: devil's advocacy and the dialectic method.

After-action review (project post-mortem): what did we intend? what actually happened? what helped or hurt? what should we do differently or keep doing? Benefits: process improvement, team cohesion, closure, morale.

summary.heading: Ch 10 · Organisational change and innovation
points: Organisational change: moving from the present state toward a desired future state.

Fundamental changes: markets are more segmented with niche products; more competitors offer targeted products, requiring faster speed-to-market; some traditional companies may not survive; offshore suppliers change the way we work; knowledge, not information, is the new competitive advantage; employees expect remote work.
Reactive change: responding to unexpected problems and opportunities. Proactive change: managing anticipated problems — introduce change before it happens.

Three forms (least → most threatening): adaptive (reintroducing a familiar practice — easiest), innovative (new to the organisation — moderate complexity, cost, uncertainty, some fear), radically innovative (new to the industry — very difficult, highly threatening).
Lewin's model: unfreezing (prepare people — they don't like change), changing (implement), refreezing (reinforce).
Systems approach: inputs → target elements of change → outputs.

Organisational development (OD) can improve individual, team and organisational performance, revitalise organisations that lost speed and innovativeness, and help adapt to mergers. Effective OD: multiple interventions (goals, training, rewards), management support, short- and long-term goals, understanding culture.

Innovation: product innovation (new or changed appearance, function or performance); incremental (improve what exists) vs radical (big change, e.g. Tesla). An innovation system is the set of mutually reinforcing structures, processes and practices that drive innovation.
Resistance to change: an emotional or behavioural response to real or imagined threats to established routines — managers help employees overcome the fear.

summary.heading: Ch 14 · Leadership and power
points: Leading: being visionary, engaging and inspiring people. Managing: using your resources to achieve goals.

Managerial leadership: influencing followers to commit to shared goals and facilitating the work to achieve them — also shown by people without a formal role (e.g. Elon Musk making seemingly impossible things).

Six sources of power: legitimate (from the formal position), reward (bonuses, extras), coercive (threats and punishment), expert (knowledge and experience), referent (charisma, attractiveness), informational (access to and control of information).

summary.heading: Ch 16 · Control and the control process
points: Controlling: monitoring performance, comparing it with goals, and taking corrective action. (Planning sets goals; organising arranges tasks, people and resources; leading motivates; controlling makes sure the right things happen at the right time in the right way.)

Six reasons for control: adapt to change and uncertainty; discover irregularities and errors; reduce costs, increase productivity or add value; detect opportunities and innovate; give performance feedback; decentralise decisions and support teamwork.
Control charts: visual statistical tool with upper and lower quality limits to monitor a process.
Management by exception: managers are informed only when data show a significant deviation from standards.
Feedforward control (future: prevent problems), concurrent control (present: real-time information), feedback control (past: after the task is done).

summary.heading: Ch 16 · Balanced scorecard
points: Measure more than financial data — four perspectives.

1 Financial: budgets (incremental — last period as reference, little flexibility; fixed — one cost estimate; variable — resources vary with activity level); financial statements (balance sheet = worth at a point in time; income statement = revenues and expenses over a period; cash flows = operating, investing, financing); financial ratios (liquidity, turnover, profitability).
2 Customer: satisfaction (meeting expectations) and retention (reduce defections — set expectations, go the extra mile, make it personal).
3 Internal business: productivity (benchmarking, best practices), efficiency, quality, safety.
4 Innovation and learning: employee attitudes, turnover (functional = underperformers leave; dysfunctional = best performers leave), resource capabilities, organisational culture.
Strategy map: visual path to organisational effectiveness.

summary.heading: Ch 16 · Quality management and contemporary issues
points: Quality control: minimise errors at each production stage. Quality assurance: focus on workers' performance, aiming for zero defects.
Deming: quality aimed at the consumer's needs; improve the system, don't blame workers; better quality → more market share and jobs; improve with hard data using PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act).

Total Quality Management (TQM): continuous improvement, involve every employee, listen to customers and employees, use accurate standards. Two core principles: people orientation (deliver customer value) and improvement orientation (continuously improve processes).
Service quality is about the customer's satisfaction — a matter of perception.

Other techniques: outsourcing; reduced cycle time; statistical process control (random samples to check quality); Six Sigma (statistical defect reduction, DMAIC: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control); Lean Six Sigma (speed with excellence).

ISO 9000: auditable quality-control procedures — customer focus, leadership, engagement of people, process approach, improvement, evidence-based decisions, relationship management. ISO 14000: environmental performance.

AI for control: productivity (predictive maintenance, safety, capacity), supply chain management, employee tracking (productivity, appropriate use of resources, theft prevention). Recommendations: start by looking inward, communicate clearly, protect privacy.
